hints.content:
The graph of $y=\sqrt[3]{x}$ can be transformed
to get the graph of $y=\sqrt[3]{5-x}+4$. 
[[☃ explanation 1]]

Let's write $y=\sqrt[3]{5-x}+4$ as $y=\sqrt[3]{-(x-5)}+4$ so that it is easier to see the transformations from the graph of $y=\sqrt[3]{x}$.

options.explanation:
Suppose $f(x)=\sqrt[3]{x}$ and $g(x)=\sqrt[3]{5-x}+4$.  

>$\begin{align}f(x)&=\sqrt[3]{x}\\\\
f(x-5)&=\sqrt[3]{x-5}\\\\
f(-(x-5))&=\sqrt[3]{-(x-5)}\\\\
f(-(x-5))+4&=\sqrt[3]{-(x-5)}+4\\\\
&=\sqrt[3]{5-x}+4
\end{align}$

Notice that what is on the right-hand side of the equal sign is $g(x)$.  Therefore, $g(x)=f(-(x-5))+4$.  

Since function $g$ can be built from function $f$, the graph of function $g$ is a transformation of the graph of function $f$.

hints.content:
Replacing $x$ with $x-5$ shifts the graph of $y=\sqrt[3]{x}$ right $5$ units.

[[☃ image 1]]

options.alt: A cube root function graph and its shifted graph on an x y coordinate plane. Its middle point is at (zero, zero). It passes through (negative eight, negative two) and (eight, two). The shifted graph's middle point is at (five, zero). It passes through (negative three, negative two) and (thirteen, two).

hints.content:
Multiplying $x-5$ by $-1$ reflects the graph of $y=\sqrt[3]{x-5}$ over the line $x=5$.


[[☃ image 1]]

options.alt: A cube root function graph and its reflected graph on an x y coordinate plane. Its middle point is at (five, zero). It passes through (negative three, negative two) and (thirteen, two). The reflected graph reflects horizontally with its middle point is at (five, zero). It passes through (negative three, two) and (thirteen, negative two).

hints.content:
Adding $4$ to the function shifts the graph of $y=\sqrt[3]{5-x}$ up $4$ units.


[[☃ image 1]]

Note that it is important to follow order of operations when building the function, as function transformations are not always commutative.  [[☃ explanation 1]]

options.explanation:
Consider the graph of $y=\sqrt{x}$.

If we shift the graph of $y=\sqrt{x}$ down $2$ units, and then reflect this across the $x$-axis, we get the following graph.

![A square root function graph on an x y coordinate plane. It has an endpoint (zero, two) and passes through (ten, negative one).](web+graphie:${☣ LOCALPATH}/images/838d19b306cd3a25ac6c67be671bb6a26eaf0e71)

However, if we first reflect the graph of $y=\sqrt{x}$ across the $x$-axis and then shift this graph down $2$ units, we get the following graph.

![A square root function graph on an x y coordinate plane. It has an endpoint (zero, negative two) and passes through (ten, negative five).](web+graphie:${☣ LOCALPATH}/images/76bbee52d28bfb5f5bcd72a6831a797eaab9824d)

These graphs are not the same, indicating that the order in which you perform the transformations is important!

options.alt: A cube root function graph and its shifted graph on an x y coordinate plane. Its middle point is at (five, zero). It passes through (negative three, two) and (thirteen, negative two). The shifted graph's middle point is at (five, four). It passes through (negative three, six) and (thirteen, two).
